title: India's 'Yo-Yo' Monsoon Whipsaws Between Drought and Deadly Floods, Threatening Crops and the Power Grid
excerpt: After weeks of El Niño-driven dry weather that slashed hydropower output by a fifth and delayed kharif sowing, torrential rains have suddenly killed at least 25 people — exposing the dangerous volatility of the 2026 monsoon season.
body:
• India's 2026 monsoon is on track to be the weakest in 11 years at 90% of the long-period average, driven by a strengthening El Niño in the Pacific.
  • Hydropower generation plunged 21% year-on-year in June, forcing coal plants to burn through an additional five million tonnes of coal in a single month.
  • After weeks of extreme dryness, torrential rains this weekend killed at least 25 people across Kashmir, Nagaland and Assam — illustrating the dangerous "yo-yo" volatility of this season.
  • Kharif sowing is delayed across 300+ vulnerable districts, and economists warn food inflation could spike to 5.5% if the erratic pattern persists through August.

India's 2026 southwest monsoon has earned an unwelcome nickname among meteorologists and commodity traders alike: the "yo-yo monsoon." Weeks of punishing dry weather that left reservoirs at their lowest levels in years have given way to sudden, violent downpours that killed at least 25 people in northern and northeastern India over the weekend, according to Reuters. The whiplash between drought and deluge is defining a season that poses a dual threat to India's food supply and its power grid.

A Season of Extremes

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast total June–September rainfall at just 90% of the 50-year long-period average (LPA), the lowest since 2015's drought year when rains fell to 86% of normal. There is an 84% probability that rainfall will be below normal this year, the agency said, after downgrading an earlier April forecast of 92%.

The culprit is a strengthening El Niño — the periodic warming of Pacific Ocean surface waters that disrupts the moisture-laden winds driving the Indian monsoon. Weather models suggest the current event could intensify to moderate or strong levels by August-September, potentially matching the devastating 2015–16 Super El Niño.

But the headline figure obscures the real danger: distribution. Cumulative monsoon rainfall was 38% below normal through July 1, according to IMD data. Then, within days, the pattern flipped. "Active monsoon conditions are likely to persist over northwest, east and northeast India during the next 6–7 days," IMD warned on Sunday, as floods swept through Poonch, Rajouri and Doda in Kashmir, killing 15. Landslides in Nagaland claimed nine more lives, while 57,000 people in Assam were affected by rising waters.

"The 166 major reservoirs tracked by the Central Water Commission held just 47.7 billion cubic metres as of July 2 — roughly a quarter of total capacity and 39% lower than a year earlier."

This erratic distribution — prolonged dry spells punctuated by torrential bursts — is what makes the 2026 monsoon especially treacherous for farmers and grid operators.

The Toll on Crops and the Power Grid

The agricultural damage is already accumulating. India's farm minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said in late June that contingency plans have been drawn up for more than 300 districts, with 111 classified as high priority because less than a quarter of their farmland has irrigation. States have been urged to shift rain-fed farmers toward short-duration, less water-intensive crops such as pulses, millets and oilseeds.

Kharif sowing of rice, corn, cotton, soybeans and sugarcane — which normally accelerates through June and July — has been delayed in many regions. "Below-normal rainfall could affect early-season planting of pulses, cotton, edible oilseeds and coarse grains such as corn," Ashwini Bansod, vice-president for commodities research at Phillip Capital India, told Reuters. Rice paddy is at particular risk in non-irrigated areas across the northern and northwestern states.

The power grid is feeling the squeeze from the other direction. Hydropower generation fell nearly 21% year-on-year in June — the steepest drop since February 2024 — according to Ministry of Power data reported by The Hindu BusinessLine. For the April–June quarter, hydro output ran 4,410 GWh below programme, with eastern India's hydro stations nearly 31% behind target, Central Electricity Authority data shows.

Reservoir storage tells the story. The 166 major reservoirs tracked by the Central Water Commission held just 47.7 billion cubic metres as of July 2 — roughly a quarter of total capacity and 39% lower than a year earlier. Thermal plants have absorbed the entire shortfall, drawing down coal stocks by five million tonnes in June alone. Electricity consumption surged 8% year-on-year in April–June, with peak demand hitting a record 270.82 GW in May amid extreme heatwaves.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRI families with agricultural land back home, the stakes are immediate. A poor kharif harvest means lower crop yields and reduced tenant-farming income. Rising vegetable and pulse prices — the items most sensitive to monsoon disruption — erode the purchasing power of remittances sent to families. Perishables such as fruits and vegetables are "the most vulnerable" to El Niño-driven heat, HSBC chief India economist Pranjul Bhandari noted in a recent report.

Travel plans are another casualty. The weekend's deadly floods in Kashmir and the northeast are a reminder that monsoon-season travel within India carries heightened risk this year, with IMD warning of active monsoon conditions persisting well into late July.

What Comes Next

The critical window is now. IMD expects July rainfall at around 94% of normal — an improvement over June's severe deficit but still below average. If August and September deliver closer to normal rains, reservoirs could partially recover and late-sown kharif crops may still salvage a reasonable harvest.

But the El Niño's trajectory remains the wild card. The Reserve Bank of India has already pared its growth forecast and raised its inflation estimate, citing monsoon risk. Gaura Sengupta, chief economist at IDFC First Bank, warned that a deficient monsoon "particularly in the crucial July-August months, can add to the pressure and push up inflation closer to an average of 5.5%." That figure compares with retail inflation of 3.48% in April.

India's US$4-trillion economy has become somewhat more resilient to monsoon shocks — 55% of gross cropped area is now irrigated, up from 40% in 2010–11, and grain buffer stocks remain ample. But the yo-yo pattern of 2026 is testing those buffers in ways a straightforward deficit would not. When the rain doesn't come, crops wilt and turbines slow. When it arrives all at once, lives are lost and topsoil washes away. For 700 million Indians who depend on farming, the worst monsoon in a decade is not just a statistic — it is a daily reckoning.
